Wales
WAYLZ
n. (the western principality of Britain, whose Reformation came by the Welsh Bible of 1588 and whose awakening came by field preaching)
Old English Wealas, the foreigners, from Proto-Germanic walhaz, a Roman or a Celt; the Welsh call their own country Cymru, the land of fellow-countrymen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wales is the western principality of Britain, and its history is the plainest case in these islands of a nation reformed by having the Scriptures put into its own tongue. The old British church held the western hills after the Saxon settlement and kept its own reckoning of Easter until the Synod of Whitby, and Augustine of Canterbury could not bring its bishops to terms. Union with England came by statute in 1536, and with it a policy that treated Welsh as a barbarism to be worn away. Against that policy Parliament passed in 1563 an act requiring the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer in Welsh. William Salesbury gave the New Testament in 1567 and Richard Davies laboured with him; William Morgan gave the whole Bible in 1588, and that book, more than any council or any prince, made a Welsh Protestant people. Rhys Prichard put doctrine into verse that labourers could carry in the head. Under the Commonwealth Vavasor Powell and Walter Cradock preached through the country, and John Penry had already died at Westminster in 1593 for pressing the want of preaching in Wales. Then Griffith Jones set up his circulating schools, teaching the poor to read the Welsh Bible, and out of that reading came Howell Harris, Daniel Rowland and William Williams. The dictionary records Wales as a nation to whom God gave the Word in its own language.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a principality as the territory of a prince; a tongue as the language of a nation; a version as a translation; vernacular as native to the country of one's birth; and a revival as renewed attention to religion.

expand to see more

PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; the territory of a prince, or the country which gives title to a prince.

TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; hence, speech; language; the whole sum of words used by a nation.

VERSION, n. A translation; the act of rendering into another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.

VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as a man's vernacular tongue.

REVIVAL, n. Return or recall to life; renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.

Key Scripture

Act 2:8 — "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

1Co 14:9 — "So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air."

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Modern Corruption

Western principality made Protestant by the Welsh Bible of 1588 and awakened by the circulating schools and the Calvinistic Methodist preachers, against both an English policy that would have extinguished the language and a modern reading that makes the result merely cultural.

expand to see more

Two corruptions meet over Wales and the dictionary names both. The first is the Tudor and Hanoverian policy that treated Welsh as a barbarous speech to be worn out of the people, leaving parishes to be served in a tongue the parishioners did not have; against it stands the apostolic wonder that men heard “how hear we every man in our own tongue” (Act 2:8), and Paul's plain rule that an unintelligible service is speech thrown away, for “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken” (1Co 14:9). The act of 1563 and Morgan's Bible of 1588 are therefore not concessions to sentiment but obedience to Scripture.

The second corruption is modern and runs the other way. It reads Welsh nonconformity as essentially a movement of national feeling that happened to wear a religious dress, so that chapel, hymn and revival become expressions of identity rather than effects of the preached Word. The record will not bear it. What changed Wales was reading: Griffith Jones taught the poor their letters so that they could read one book, and the men converted at those desks preached. Nehemiah's pattern is the Welsh pattern, where they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8), and Paul's question is the Welsh question, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). A nation is not awakened by pride in itself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dialektos (G1258), a tongue or language; Greek eusemos (G2154), easy to be understood; Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach as a herald.

expand to see more

Greek dialektos (G1258) — a language, the speech of a people; “how hear we every man in our own tongue”, Acts 2:8.

Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget, to be born; “wherein we were born”, Acts 2:8.

Greek eusemos (G2154) — well-marked, significant, easy to be understood; “words easy to be understood”, 1 Corinthians 14:9.

Greek glossa (G1100) — the tongue, a language; “except ye utter by the tongue”, 1 Corinthians 14:9.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald, to preach; “how shall they hear without a preacher?”, Romans 10:14.

Usage

"“how hear we every man in our own tongue” (Act 2:8) — the act of 1563 requiring the Welsh Bible and Prayer Book."

"“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — Griffith Jones's circulating schools."

"“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — John Penry's complaint, for which he died in 1593."
